section.title: Differentiability and continuity
section.p: Differentiability requires that a curve locally resembles a straight line. Because lines cannot jump, any differentiable function must necessarily be continuous: differentiability is strictly stronger than continuity.

statement.p: If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.

proof.p: Since f'(a) exists as a finite real number, for h\neq 0 we write:
Hence \lim_{h\to 0}f(a+h) = f(a), proving that f is continuous at a.

subsection.title: Why the converse is false
subsection.p: Continuity ensures that a curve does not break; differentiability demands a single limiting tangent slope. A curve can be connected without possessing a unique tangent slope.

subsection.title: The absolute value as the first warning example
subsection.p: For f(x)=|x|, no single linear approximation |h| \approx mh can satisfy \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{|h|-mh}{h} = 0, because the left slope is -1 and the right slope is +1.

subsection.title: A note about endpoints
subsection.p: The standard derivative definition requires a two-sided limit. At boundary endpoints of intervals (e.g. x=0 for \sqrt{x} on [0,\infty)), only one-sided derivative limits can be formed.
